t: Early societies urged moderate drinking, which is why the movement bears the name temperance; from the 1830s teetotalism demanded complete abstinence, and later reformers sought laws against the sale of alcohol.
By 1900, scholars have estimated, one in ten Americans had signed a pledge to abstain, and the movement became the most well-organised lobby group of its time.

National prohibitions were introduced in Canada, Norway, Finland and the United States between 1918 and 1920 and were repealed, the American one in 1933, after critics pointed to bootlegging, crime and lost tax revenue.
dyk: In 1767 the average New England family was consuming seven barrels of hard cider a year, about 35 gallons per person, in the colonies where the temperance movement later took shape.
ev: The American Temperance Society is formed in Boston, and within 12 years claims more than 8,000 local groups and over 1,250,000 members
Teetotalism originates in Preston, Lancashire, and William Apess founds the first formal Native American temperance society among the Maspee
Artisans in Baltimore found the Washingtonians, who pledge complete abstinence and rely on sympathy for drinkers rather than on law
Maine passes a full-fledged prohibition law, the work of Neal Dow, and several other states follow in the next two decades
A crusade against saloons begins in Ohio, and the Woman's Christian Temperance Union is organised in Cleveland the next year
The Anti-Saloon League begins in Ohio and later campaigns for national prohibition
The Eighteenth Amendment introduces prohibition of the manufacture, sale and distribution of alcoholic beverages in the United States
The Twenty-first Amendment is ratified on 5 December and repeals nationwide prohibition

f.where: the United States, Great Britain and Ireland, the British colonies including Australia, New Zealand and India, Canada, Norway, Finland, Iceland, Russia and France
f.period: earlier efforts from 1737 and the 1790s; a national movement in the United States from the 1820s; teetotalism from the 1830s; the Washingtonians from 1840; gospel temperance after the American Civil War; a mass movement from the 1860s; national prohibitions in the 1910s and 1920s; decline from the 1930s; still active today
f.figures: Benjamin Rush, physician who described drinking as a disease; Lyman Beecher, minister who called drunkenness a national sin; John Edgar, Belfast minister; Theobald Mathew, Irish priest; Neal Dow, behind the Maine law of 1851; Frances Willard, second president of the Woman's Christian Temperance Union; Carrie Nation, arrested 30 times; Wayne Wheeler of the Anti-Saloon League
f.outcome: national prohibitions in Canada, Norway, Finland and the United States, all later repealed, and prohibition in some Indian provinces from 1948 to the present; the movement still exists, with less political influence than in the early 20th century
